newsitem.title: USA: IMM currency futures erode gains, end higher.
newsitem.headline: IMM currency futures erode gains, end higher.

text.p: IMM currency futures eroded gains again late, but most still finished pit trading higher.

Turnover picked up again after a brief lull when already holiday-thinned European trade shut, although afternoon price moves were more contained as the market eyed a full slate of economic events next week.

On Tuesday, the Federal Reserve's Open Market Committee meets to consider U.S. rates and monetary policy. Although few analysts or traders expect the U.S. central bank to raise rates, the slightest uncertainty provided a convenient pre-weekend excuse to even up, they said.
Also on Tuesday, the market will discover what plans the Bundesbank has for short rates when it announces its weekly securities repurchase tender.

Analysts were divided over the whether the German central bank will switch to a variable rate repo for the first time in a year. They said the market would interpret such a move as a signal of the Buba's readiness to hike official rates as well, possibly at Thursday's first post-recess council meeting.
Yen retraced only a tiny portion of the week's big losses, as it slammed into a ceiling Friday at $0.008600, exactly where a fund had sold some 2,000 contracts Thursday.
Brokers expected yen to continue moving lower, given the spillover from problems battering Southeast Asian currencies, technicals and crosses with currencies offering higher yields.
The yen's inability to hold on to the bulk of Friday's early gains also persuaded some players to bail out, at least until the market see Japan's July trade figures, due Sunday,
They said surge higher in sterling came partly at the expense of yen, with the U.K. government proving unable to quell buying enthusiasm for the pound.
"The pound has a good economy (behind it) and...they can't talk it down for long," said one floor broker.

Currencies rallied abruptly Friday morning as the dollar slumped below key technical levels and U.S. Treasury bonds and stocks extended losses, although brokers in those two markets pointed to the dollar's decline as partly responsible for their moves lower.

September yen ended up $0.000009 at $0.008519, marks gained $0.0045 to $0.5488, Swiss francs rose $0.0042 to $0.6654, Sterling advanced $0.000184 to $01.6054, Canadian dollar added $0.0004 to $0.7206, Aussie dollar rose $0.0018 to $0.7435, and the Mexican peso lost $0.000025 to $0.127300.
